title: Navigating Strategic Inertia in Local Legislatures: Role of Public Leadership in Overcoming Bureaucratic Passivity
content: Local legislatures play a critical role in lawmaking, budgeting, oversight, and translating societal demands into public policy, yet formal decentralization may coexist with executive dominance, information asymmetry, strategic inertia, and bureaucratic passivity. This study examines how executive dominance contributes to strategic inertia in Indonesian local legislatures and explores how public leadership and multidimensional institutional capacities can facilitate transformation toward substantive public value. A qualitative comparative-exploratory multiple-case study was conducted involving 35 informants selected through purposive and supplementary snowball sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, non-participant observation, and documentary analysis and examined using comparative thematic analysis incorporating open, axial, selective, and cross-case coding. Five interconnected themes emerged: executive dominance and structural dependence; strategic inertia and bureaucratic passivity; public leadership as a mechanism for disrupting inertia; multidimensional institutional, individual, budgetary, and regulatory capacity; and the transition from procedural compliance to substantive public value. The findings indicate that leadership can disrupt entrenched legislative routines, but sustainable transformation depends on complementary institutional capacities that strengthen autonomy, inclusion, responsiveness, and accountability. The study contributes an integrated explanatory framework linking structural dependence, organizational inertia, public leadership, multidimensional capacity strengthening, and substantive public value in local legislative governance.
